'''''Tulipa gesneriana''''', the '''Didier's tulip'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TUGE|taxon=Tulipa gesneriana|accessdate=12 December 2015}}</ref> or '''garden tulip''', is a species of plant in the [[Liliaceae|lily family]], cultivated as an ornamental in many countries because of its large, showy flowers. This tall, late-blooming species has a single blooming flower and linear or broadly [[lanceolate]] leaves. This is a complex hybridized neo-species, and can also be called ''Tulipa'' × ''gesneriana''.<ref>Maarten J. M. Christenhusz, Rafaël Govaerts, John C. David, Tony Hall, Katherine Borland, Penelope S. Roberts, Anne Tuomisto, Sven Buerki, Mark W. Chase, Michael F. Fay, Tiptoe through the tulips – cultural history, molecular phylogenetics and classification of Tulipa (Liliaceae). Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society 172, 2013, 312</ref> Most of the [[cultivar]]s of tulip are derived from ''Tulipa gesneriana''. It has become naturalised in parts of central and southern [[Europe]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=tulipa+gesneriana|title=Tulipa gesneriana [Tulipano di von Gesner] - Flora Italiana|website=luirig.altervista.org|access-date=25 May 2019}}</ref> and scattered locations in [[North America]].<ref>{{BONAP |genus=Tulipa |species=gesneriana |date=2014 |access-date=25 May 2019}}</ref>[[File:Illustration of Tulipa gesneriana.jpg|thumb|left|Illustration and excerpt of ''Tulipa gesneriana''.]]

==Description==
===Vegetative characteristics===
''Tulipa gesneriana'' is a bulbous<ref name = "POWO">''Tulipa gesneriana'' L. (n.d.). Plants of the World Online. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:542923-1</ref> herb<ref name = "VASCAN">''Tulipa gesneriana'' Linnaeus. (n.d.). Database of Vascular Plants of Canada (VASCAN). Retrieved January 13, 2025, from https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/28720</ref> with ovate-lanceolate leaves.<ref name = "Linnaeus, 1753" /> The bulb produces offsets laterally.<ref name = "Botanical Register" />
===Generative characteristics===
The erect, broadly campanulate flowers<ref name = "Botanical Register" /> with glabrous, obtuse tepals<ref name = "Rothmaler">Müller, F., Ritz, C. M., Wesche, K., & Welk, E. (2021). [https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-662-61011-4 Rothmaler - Exkursionsflora von Deutschland. Gefäßpflanzen: Grundband.] p. 153. Springer Spektrum.</ref> have six stamens and three carpels.<ref name = "Botanical Register">[https://archive.org/details/botanicalregiste05edwa/page/n139/mode/2up The Botanical Register : consisting of coloured figures of exotic plants, cultivated in British gardens; with their history and mode of treatment (Vol. 5).] (1819)</ref>

The specific epithet ''gesneriana'' honours the Swiss botanist [[Conrad Gesner]].<ref name = "Grout">Grout, J. (n.d.). Conrad Gesner. Encyclopaedia Romana. ==Ecology==
The flowers are pollinated by ''[[Halictus]]'' bees.<ref name = "Loew, 1892">E. Loew. (1892). [https://www.google.de/books/edition/Jahrb%C3%BCcher_f%C3%BCr_wissenschaftliche_Botan/rtm6vvyCH0MC?hl=de&gbpv=1&dq=Tulipa%20gesneriana&pg=PA230&printsec=frontcover Blüthenbiologische Beiträge II.] Jahrbücher Für Wissenschaftliche Botanik, 23, 207–253.</ref> 
[[File:SEM_Image_of_Tulip_Pollen.jpg|thumb|BSD SEM of Pollen Captured off Tulip Petal.]]

==History==
This hybrid is widely believed to have originated in [[Tian Shan]] of [[Central Asia]], from the collections of the sultan of the [[Ottoman Empire]] in Istanbul, as is the case with other species of [[tulip]]s that came into [[Europe]].<ref name=s/> In 1574, Sultan [[Selim II]] ordered the Kadi of [[Azaz|A‘azāz]] in Syria to send him 50,000 tulip bulbs. However, Harvey points out several problems with this source, and there is also the possibility that tulips and [[Hyacinth (plant)|hyacinth]] (''sümbül''), originally Indian [[spikenard]] (''Nardostachys jatamansi'') have been confused.<ref name="Harvey">{{cite journal |first=John H. |last=Harvey |year=1976 |title=Turkey as a Source of Garden Plants |journal=Garden History |volume=4 |issue=3 |page=24 |doi=10.2307/1586521 |jstor=1586521 }}</ref> Sultan Selim also imported 300,000 bulbs of ''Kefe Lale'' (also known as Cafe-Lale, from the medieval name Kaffa, probably ''[[Tulipa sauveolens]]'', syn. ''Tulipa schrenkii'') from the port of [[Feodossija|Kefe]] in [[Crimea]], for his gardens in the  [[Topkapı Palace|Topkapı Sarayı]] in [[Istanbul]]. They are hybridized with other species present in the collections.<ref>{{cite book |first=Anna |last=Pavord |title=The Tulip |url=https://archive.org/details/tulippavo00pavo |url-access=registration |location=London |publisher=Bloomsbury |year=1999 |page=[https://archive.org/details/tulippavo00pavo/page/41 41]|isbn=9781582340135 }}</ref> ''Tulipa sauveolens'' is genetically very closely related to ''Tulipa gesneriana'', and sometimes classified in the same species.

''Tulipa gesneriana'' was introduced to western Europe from [[Constantinople]] in 1554. It was first described in 1559 by [[Conrad Gesner]].<ref name=Wilson>[[John Marius Wilson|Rev. John Marius Wilson]] (Editor) {{google books|pVE9AQAAMAAJ|The Rural Cyclopedia: Or A General Dictionary of Agriculture, and of the Arts, Sciences, Instruments and Practise, necessary to the farmer, stockfarmer, gardener, forester, landsteward, farrier, &c. Volume 4, (1857)|page=498}}</ref>
[[File:Stereoscope_Image_of_Tulip_Anatomy.jpg|thumb|Tulip stereoscope image demonstrating anther, filament, and petal. Pollen visible in background.]]
When the tulip originally arrived in Europe from the Ottoman Empire, its popularity soared and it quickly became a status symbol for the newly wealthy merchants of the [[Dutch Golden Age]]. As a [[mosaic virus]] began to infect bulbs, producing rare and spectacular effects in the bloom but weakening and destroying the already limited number of bulbs, a speculative frenzy now known as [[tulip mania]] was triggered between 1634 and 1637. Bulbs were exchanged for land, livestock, and houses, and the Dutch created [[Futures exchange|futures markets]] where contracts to buy bulbs at the end of the season were bought and sold.<ref>Goldgar, Anne, ''Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age'', University of Chicago Press, p. 322.</ref> A single bulb, the ''Semper Augustus'', fetched 6,000 florins in [[Haarlem]] — at that time, a florin could purchase a bushel of wheat.

==Use==
===Food===
The flower and bulb can cause dermatitis through the [[allergen]], tuliposide A, even though the bulbs may be consumed with little ill effect. The bulbs may be dried and pulverised and added to cereals or flour.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gette |first=M. T. |last2=Marks |first2=J. E. |date=February 1990 |title=Tulip fingers |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2137323 |journal=Archives of Dermatology |volume=126 |issue=2 |pages=203–205 |issn=0003-987X |pmid=2137323}}</ref>
[[File:Tulipe des jardins - Tulipa gesneriana.jpg|thumb|Tulip plant at the beginning of March]]
[[File:Tulipe des jardins (Tulipa gesneriana) ouverte vers midijpg.jpg|thumb|Tulip open around noon]]

===Horticulture===
The sweet-scented bisexual flowers appear during April and May. Bulbs are extremely resistant to frost and can tolerate temperatures well below freezing — a period of low temperature is necessary to induce proper growth and flowering, triggered by an increase in sensitivity to the [[phytohormone]] [[auxin]].<ref>Rietveld, Patrick L.; Wilkinson, Claire; Franssen, Hanneke M.; Balk, Peter A.; van der Plas, Linus H.W.; Weisbeek,  Peter J.; de Boer, A. Douwe, "Low temperature sensing in tulip (''Tulipa gesneriana'' L.) is mediated through an increased response to auxin", ''Journal of Experimental Botany'', v.51, no. 344, March, 2000, p. 587-594.</ref>
